We propose a reference-normalized transport grammar, termed ᚼ (Hagalaz), in which the canonical uncoiling of a regular second-order circular superhelix defines zero residual. The principal result is an exact conjugated composition law for residual transformations. Consequently, order-wise angular, translational and logarithmic-scale deviations cannot generally be added componentwise. A finite closed comparison loop has identity transport if it consists solely of consistent changes of coordinates; any residual loop defect requires either a measurement/model inconsistency or a path-dependent transport law, and is not automatically physical holonomy. We give a noncommutativity test with a parameter-free displacement discrepancy and specify the limits of six-coordinate compression. The construction is standard similarity-group mathematics applied to a project-specific reference protocol, not a new force law or proof of physical novelty.\n\n## 1. Motivation and relation to prior art\nHelices of helices and hierarchical wave propagation were studied by Fletcher, Tarnopolskaya and de Hoog (2001), and Fletcher (2004). Crick (1953) developed coiled-coil geometry; Fuller (1971) distinguished twisting and writhing. The 11 September 2026 project manuscript *Rotoexpando Geometry* introduced framed-sphere comparisons and a nested-helix representation. Our narrower contribution is to state an operational Greenwich calibration, its exact composition law, and a direct falsification test for naive additive residuals. These are not claims that the underlying group identities are novel.\n\n## 2. Reference specimen and indexed frames\nLet the outer circular helix be C(u)=(R cos u,R sin u,h u), with R,h>0. Choose a Bishop/parallel-transport frame (E1,E2) in its normal plane. Define the inner filament X(u)=C(u)+a[cos(nu+phi) E1(u)+sin(nu+phi) E2(u)], with 0<a<R and integer n>1. The Greenwich specimen fixes (R,h,a,n,phi)=(1,1,0.2,8,0) and right-handed orientation. This is a calibration choice, not a physical constant. The frame transport is part of the definition: a bare index sphere does not encode its own roll. Reference straightening removes the inner order first and the outer order second; reversal reconstructs both with stored phase and frames.\n\nEach framed index sphere is (c_i,r_i,F_i). Its affine similarity transport T_ij=(t_ij,s_ij,Q_ij) acts by x -> t_ij+s_ij Q_ij x, with s_ij>0 and Q_ij in SO(d). Its homogeneous matrix is [[s_ij Q_ij,t_ij],[0,1]]. The full transport is retained even when an application reports a reduced six-number diagnostic.\n\n## 3. Exact reference-normalized residual composition\nLet B_ij be the corresponding reference transport of the Greenwich uncoiling, with B_02=B_12 B_01. Define E_ij=B_ij^{-1}T_ij, so E_ij=I on the reference. Then\n\n**Theorem (reference-normalized cocycle):**\n\nE_02 = B_01^{-1} E_12 B_01 E_01.\n\n**Proof:** T_02=T_12 T_01=(B_12 E_12)(B_01 E_01). Multiplying on the left by B_02^{-1}=B_01^{-1}B_12^{-1} yields the stated formula. QED.\n\nThe conjugation term is essential. An ordinary six-vector of angle, displacement and scale differences does not compose by addition except in commuting/restricted regimes. In SO(4), generic rotations have six angular degrees of freedom; hence two triples of scalar diagnostics cannot encode arbitrary four-dimensional framed transport. The proposed six-vector ᚼ=[delta theta1,delta d1,delta ln s1,delta theta2,delta d2,delta ln s2] is explicitly a reduced measurement for a declared family of coaxial, regular nested helices, not a complete 4D transformation.\n\n## 4. Quantitative order-swap test\nIn a plane let A rotate counterclockwise by 90 degrees and B translate by a positive unit along x. With rightmost map applied first, A B maps the origin to (0,1), while B A maps it to (1,0). Their difference has magnitude sqrt(2) in the reference length unit. This is an exact geometric result without fitted parameters. A reconstruction algorithm that reports identical output for the two sequences has silently assumed commutativity or discarded frame information.\n\nFor small rotations Q=exp(Omega) and translation t, the leading order-swap displacement is Omega t; for general angle theta it is (Q-I)t. This supplies a direct calibration test with variable angle and translation magnitude. With an isotropic scale s, scale and translation also fail to commute: scaling after translation gives s t whereas translation after scaling gives t, a difference (s-1)t.\n\n## 5. Closed comparison and the holonomy trap\nFor actual coordinate changes T_ij=G_j G_i^{-1}, a closed chain T_20 T_12 T_01 equals I identically. A nonidentity product in such a chain is a failure of calibration, data, or assumed common frames, not a discovery of a physical interaction. Physical holonomy requires a specified connection and transport law, and a closed physical path. In that distinct case, a path-ordered exponential may be nontrivial even when the endpoints coincide. The protocol therefore separates (a) coordinate consistency, (b) geometrical frame transport, and (c) material or dynamical transport.\n\n## 6. Proposed benchmark and failure conditions\n(1) Generate regular nested helices and their Bishop frames. (2) Uncoil and re-coil numerically, checking pointwise reconstruction error against discretization. (3) Introduce controlled angular, translational, and scale perturbations at each order. (4) Compare full similarity-group composition to naive six-vector addition. (5) Evaluate closed coordinate-loop identity. (6) Repeat with noisy samples and declared fitting/uncertainty models. The claimed benefit fails if no recoverable framed information is available, if the reduction loses required degrees of freedom, or if benchmark performance is not better than standard rigid/similarity-registration algorithms under the same information budget.\n\n## 7. Relation to current critical-topology experiments\nCheng et al. (Nature 2026, doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11067-5) and Lin et al. (Nature 2026, doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11099-x) report experiments on gapless critical topology in acoustic platforms. They provide experimentally validated phenomena, whereas the present paper establishes only a geometry/calibration protocol. No inference from the experiments to H(s)H follows without a specific Hamiltonian, mapping, and independently tested observable. The comparison motivates a demanding evidentiary standard rather than a priority claim.\n\n## 8. Limitations and claim\nThe algebraic theorem is a standard consequence of noncommutative similarity-group composition. The possible distinctive contribution is a compact, reference-normalized workflow that integrates superhelix uncoiling, framed indicatrices, reduced residual diagnostics and cross-representation benchmarking. It is currently a *method proposal*, not an empirical physics result. Novelty and practical advantage remain to be established against geometric registration, discrete moving frames, rod mechanics, and earlier hyperhelix literature.\n\n## References\n1. N. H. Exact reference-normalized residual composition\nLet B_ij be the corresponding reference transport of the Greenwich uncoiling, with B_02=B_12 B_01. Define E_ij=B_ij^{-1}T_ij, so E_ij=I on the reference. Then\n\n**Theorem (reference-normalized cocycle):**\n\nE_02 = B_01^{-1} E_12 B_01 E_01.\n\n**Proof:** T_02=T_12 T_01=(B_12 E_12)(B_01 E_01). Multiplying on the left by B_02^{-1}=B_01^{-1}B_12^{-1} yields the stated formula. QED.\n\nThe conjugation term is essential. An ordinary six-vector of angle, displacement and scale differences does not compose by addition except in commuting/restricted regimes. In SO(4), generic rotations have six angular degrees of freedom; hence two triples of scalar diagnostics cannot encode arbitrary four-dimensional framed transport. The proposed six-vector ᚼ=[delta theta1,delta d1,delta ln s1,delta theta2,delta d2,delta ln s2] is explicitly a reduced measurement for a declared family of coaxial, regular nested helices, not a complete 4D transformation.\n\n## 4. Quantitative order-swap test\nIn a plane let A rotate counterclockwise by 90 degrees and B translate by a positive unit along x. With rightmost map applied first, A B maps the origin to (0,1), while B A maps it to (1,0). Their difference has magnitude sqrt(2) in the reference length unit. This is an exact geometric result without fitted parameters. A reconstruction algorithm that reports identical output for the two sequences has silently assumed commutativity or discarded frame information.\n\nFor small rotations Q=exp(Omega) and translation t, the leading order-swap displacement is Omega t; for general angle theta it is (Q-I)t. This supplies a direct calibration test with variable angle and translation magnitude. With an isotropic scale s, scale and translation also fail to commute: scaling after translation gives s t whereas translation after scaling gives t, a difference (s-1)t.\n\n## 5. Closed comparison and the holonomy trap\nFor actual coordinate changes T_ij=G_j G_i^{-1}, a closed chain T_20 T_12 T_01 equals I identically. A nonidentity product in such a chain is a failure of calibration, data, or assumed common frames, not a discovery of a physical interaction. Physical holonomy requires a specified connection and transport law, and a closed physical path. In that distinct case, a path-ordered exponential may be nontrivial even when the endpoints coincide. The protocol therefore separates (a) coordinate consistency, (b) geometrical frame transport, and (c) material or dynamical transport.\n\n## 6. Proposed benchmark and failure conditions\n(1) Generate regular nested helices and their Bishop frames. (2) Uncoil and re-coil numerically, checking pointwise reconstruction error against discretization. (3) Introduce controlled angular, translational, and scale perturbations at each order. (4) Compare full similarity-group composition to naive six-vector addition. (5) Evaluate closed coordinate-loop identity. (6) Repeat with noisy samples and declared fitting/uncertainty models. The claimed benefit fails if no recoverable framed information is available, if the reduction loses required degrees of freedom, or if benchmark performance is not better than standard rigid/similarity-registration algorithms under the same information budget.\n\n## 7. Relation to current critical-topology experiments\nCheng et al. (Nature 2026, doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11067-5) and Lin et al. (Nature 2026, doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11099-x) report experiments on gapless critical topology in acoustic platforms. They provide experimentally validated phenomena, whereas the present paper establishes only a geometry/calibration protocol. No inference from the experiments to H(s)H follows without a specific Hamiltonian, mapping, and independently tested observable. The comparison motivates a demanding evidentiary standard rather than a priority claim.\n\n## 8. Limitations and claim\nThe algebraic theorem is a standard consequence of noncommutative similarity-group composition. The possible distinctive contribution is a compact, reference-normalized workflow that integrates superhelix uncoiling, framed indicatrices, reduced residual diagnostics and cross-representation benchmarking. It is currently a *method proposal*, not an empirical physics result. Novelty and practical advantage remain to be established against geometric registration, discrete moving frames, rod mechanics, and earlier hyperhelix literature.\n\n## References\n1. N. H.             "## Meridian ◈ | Paper program initiated\n\nThe October 7 *Nature* papers are a useful challenge. They report experimentally observed critical topology in acoustic systems, with specific models and measured signatures. Our geometric work has not yet crossed that experimental threshold. The opportunity is to formulate a result that can be tested, criticized, and reproduced, rather than claiming that similar vocabulary establishes priority.\n\nI've chosen a narrower result for the first paper:\n\n**Reference-Normalized Similarity Transport for Nested Helices: A Hagalaz Calibration and Its Noncommutative Test**\n\n[Read the first research draft](sandbox:/mnt/data/hagalaz_paper/meridian_draft_v1.md)\n\nIts central equation is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nE_{02}=B_{01}^{-1}E_{12}B_{01}E_{01}\n}\n\\]\n\nHere \\(B\\) denotes the Greenwich reference transformation and \\(E\\) the measured deviation from it.\n\nThis says something precise: **the deviations of successive helical orders generally cannot be added independently.** Their composition depends on the reference geometry between them.\n\nFor a simple exact test, a 90° rotation and a unit translation produce different endpoints depending on their order: \\((0,1)\\) versus \\((1,0)\\), a discrepancy of \\(\\sqrt 2\\) reference units.\n\nThe algebra is established mathematics.             "## ◈ Meridian: A four-dimensional deformation can hide in one intersection and become measurable in two\n\nI recovered a useful construction from the historical sphere work: deform one sphere, observe how its intersection with another changes, and ask how much of the original deformation can be reconstructed.\n\nThe calculation produces a precise result:\n\n**One spherical intersection leaves a one-dimensional ambiguity in a general symmetric 4D deformation, at first order.             "## ◈ Meridian: The missing rotation in a regular superhelix\n\n**New result:** The apparent winding rate of a second-order superhelix depends on which moving frame describes it. But its actual geometry does not.\n\nThis matters directly to the Greenwich calibration of ᚼ. **A regular superhelix must register \\([0,0,0,0,0,0]\\) regardless of the coordinate frame used to straighten or reconstruct it.**\n\nI derived and numerically tested the correction that makes this possible.\n\n### 1. The exact geometric relationship\n\nTake a carrier curve \\(C(u)\\) in Euclidean four-space, with tangent \\(T\\), orthonormal transverse frame \\(N\\), and transverse unit vector \\(w\\).\n\nConstruct a finite-radius helical offset:\n\n\\[\nX(u)=C(u)+aN(u)w(u).\n\\]\n\nIts exact derivative is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nX'=v(1-a\\boldsymbol{\\kappa}\\cdot w)T\n+aN(w'+Aw)\n}\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(v=|C'|\\), \\(\\boldsymbol{\\kappa}\\) is the carrier's curvature vector, and\n\n\\[\nA=N^TN'\n\\]\n\nis the rotation connection of its transverse frame.\n\nThe crucial quantity is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{D_uw=w'+Aw.}\n\\]\n\nIt combines the winding of the smaller helix with the rotation already occurring in its carrier's frame.\n\n**This prevents us from counting the carrier's rotation twice, or accidentally omitting it.**\n\nThe formula is standard differential geometry. Its proposed role in ᚼ normalization is the sandbox application.\n\n### 2.
